title: A virtue gripped too hard
hookLine: Montaigne distrusts extremes, even in virtue
carry: even a virtue, gripped too hard, becomes a fault

cards: A friend starts running. Good. Then it's every morning, then twice a day, then the knees give out and the running stops completely.

Another friend decides to be honest, really honest, and within a week has told three people exactly what's wrong with their haircuts, their marriages and their cooking. Both goals were good. Something went wrong anyway.
Montaigne has an essay about exactly this, and it says something unexpected: you can hold even a virtue too tightly.

teach.h: AS IF OUR TOUCH WERE INFECTIOUS.
teach.b: First, the image. In the essay Of moderation, Montaigne says it's as if our touch were infectious. We take hold of things that are good in themselves and spoil them by how we handle them.

We can grip virtue so hard, he says, with such violent desire, that it turns into a fault. He knows the objection: some say there can't be too much virtue, because once it's excessive it isn't virtue anymore.
Montaigne calls that playing with words. In real life, people do overdo good things. Third, his witness.
He points to a line of Saint Paul, from the letter to the Romans.
In the King James Bible it reads: "not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think soberly."
Montaigne hears in it a call to be wise with measure, not to push even wisdom past its proper size. Fourth, what this asks.
Not to care less. He isn't asking anyone to be lukewarm about being kind or honest or healthy.

He's asking for a grip that doesn't crush what it holds: honesty that still leaves the other person standing, discipline that still leaves the knees working, devotion that still leaves room for dinner with friends.

how: In the essay Of moderation, Montaigne argues that even good things, virtue included, can be spoiled by being grasped too violently, and he appeals to Saint Paul's call to think soberly.

o: a warning that even a virtue can be gripped too hard
a rule to eat and drink only half of what you're served
a call to care less about being kind or honest

games.q: someone tells Montaigne: excess virtue isn't virtue, so you can't have too much of it. what does he say?
o: that's playing with words; people really do overdo good things.
games.why: he calls it playing with words. in real life, he says, we can seize virtue so violently that it becomes a fault.

practice: Notice your hands; if they're clenched at all, let them loosen.

Bring to mind one good thing you've been gripping hard lately, work, a diet, a cause, helping someone, being right, and hold it the way you'd hold a bird: firmly enough that it stays, gently enough that it breathes.
